summary:
Sergipe stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted on a 14-1 vote; joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full equal rights from 2015; and a person may change their name and gender marker without surgery, hormones or a diagnosis under the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018. A trans visitor's documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in matters of marriage and adoption.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. Brazilian courts have applied that provision to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing. An expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide.

No third-gender option exists in national identity documents. Civil registries have nevertheless been able to record 'non-binary/unspecified' entries since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of the registry to a neutral gender, established as precedent for lower courts.

The statutory text does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country report of 12 March 2026 records that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, trans people above all, and that the legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The same report notes that gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

Enforcement also varies geographically. The April 2026 law-firm guide reports that major cities including São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. Sergipe's smaller municipalities fall on the less-resourced side of that division.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. A judge fixes the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, setting out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and asking trans, travesti and intersex people which they prefer, and within it whether the general population or a specific wing or cell. The preference is recorded, later changes of placement are possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in one large state's metropolitan prison system, finding that travestis and trans women are held in units operated as masculine, some in so-called neutral or security units, and characterising placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Protection machinery has widened in parallel: analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.
tangentialFactors:
Political visibility of trans people in Brazil has risen sharply. Salabert and Hilton were elected in 2022 as the country's first transgender federal legislators, and over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections. In the October 2024 municipal cycle close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Violence has also been documented in settings a visitor would use. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists.

Trans voters may register under their lived name and identity even before their documents are updated, an accommodation that extends to candidates as well as voters.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Sergipe-specific source in the inventory records incidents of violence against trans people, court applications of Law 7.716/1989 within the state, or the placement decisions of Sergipe's own detaining authorities; the enforcement pattern described here is drawn from national reporting and from one other state's prison census.

Whether Sergipe's civil registry offices in practice issue non-binary entries, and how quickly gender-marker changes are processed there, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The inventory gives no figures for the number of openly LGBTQ candidates in Sergipe's municipal elections, and no state-level tally for the threats reported against trans candidates in October 2024.

How often judges in Sergipe consult an arrested trans person about placement preference, and whether LGBTI-specific units exist in the state's facilities at all, is not addressed by the available sources.
